title: YawnClear
question: Why do we yawn?
hook: You probably yawned before you were born, and reading this might make you yawn now. Scrub through one six-second yawn, test the oxygen myth, see the brain-cooling idea and its thermal window, and watch a yawn spread around a room.

explainer.title: A fixed six-second routine
explainer.text: A yawn is a built-in sequence: the jaw drops wide with a long, deep breath in, a short peak where the face stretches and the eyes close, then a quicker breath out. A typical adult yawn lasts about 6 seconds, though single yawns vary.

explainer.title: Not about oxygen
explainer.text: The popular idea that we yawn for more oxygen has weak support. In 1987 Robert Provine and colleagues found that breathing air with extra carbon dioxide, or exercising, made people breathe harder but not yawn more, and pure oxygen did not stop yawns.

explainer.title: Maybe a brain cooler
explainer.text: A leading hypothesis (Gallup and Gallup, 2007) is that yawning helps cool the brain by boosting blood flow and drawing in air. It predicts a thermal window: most yawning when the air is mild, less when it is freezing or as hot as the body. It is still debated.

explainer.title: Switching gears
explainer.text: We yawn most around waking, before sleep and when bored. One idea is that yawns help shift the body between states of alertness. No single explanation is settled, and yawning may do more than one job.

explainer.title: Catching yawns
explainer.text: Seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can trigger one. Roughly 40 to 60 percent of adults catch yawns in lab studies, and yawns spread most between family and friends. Its link with empathy is debated.

explainer.title: Old and widespread
explainer.text: Fish, reptiles, birds and mammals have been seen to yawn, and dogs can catch yawns from people. Across mammals, species with bigger brains tend to yawn for longer. Humans yawn in the womb from about 11 to 12 weeks, but only start catching yawns at around 4 or 5.

concepts.def: An involuntary wide opening of the mouth with a long, deep breath in, a brief peak and a shorter breath out.
A built-in sequence of movements that, once started, usually runs to the end.
A proposed explanation that can be tested and could turn out wrong.
The idea that yawning helps keep the brain at its best working temperature.
The prediction that yawning is most common at moderate air temperatures.
Yawning set off by seeing, hearing, reading or thinking about someone else yawning.
Yawning with no outside trigger, for example when tired or bored.
Yawns spread more easily between people, or animals, who know each other well.
The tube linking the middle ear to the throat, which a yawn can open, making the ears pop.
